title: Edge-case queueing and GPU fragmentation lab notes
body:
Purpose:
This is a lab-style writeup of a small-scale POC that reproduces pathological latency and cost outcomes caused by high rates of very short LLM requests (30–300ms generation) that interact poorly with GPU allocation granularity, KV-cache fragmentation, and our autoscaler cooldowns. Goal was to identify mitigations that reduce per-token cost and 95th/99th latency without increasing reserved capacity commit too much.

Background and motivation:
- Customer context: mid-market SaaS app with chat suggestions at token-level (many tiny completions per user interaction) and spiky traffic from batch imports. They saw high costs and tail latency despite low average utilization.
- Hypothesis: lots of short-lived requests cause GPUs to be underfilled (slot fragmentation), warmup overheads dominate, and autoscaler oscillation amplifies cost.

Experiment setup:
- Runtime: local staging cluster (3 node types) running the inference engine branch with logging hooks.
- Hardware mix: simulated pool with A10G-equivalent pricing for cost calcs; nodes simulated as "small" (1xGPU), "tall" (4xGPU).
- Workload generator: produced poisson bursts and periodic microrequests:
  - micro: 40k reqs/hour, payloads ~10 tokens gen (30–120ms serve time when batched)
  - medium: 4k reqs/hour, payloads ~60–200 tokens (500ms–1.2s)
  - bursts: 1000 reqs over 2 minutes (mixed sizes)
- Measurement: per-request latency distribution, GPU occupancy timeslice (50ms resolution), KV-cache hit ratio, and autoscaler decision traces. Cost model: $3.20/hr per A10G-equivalent GPU (on-demand); reserved discounts modeled separately.

Key observations:
1) Fragmentation metric: when many micro requests arrive, GPUs show 40–60% effective slot utilization because small requests occupy whole timeslices leaving many gaps that could have been packed. This is worse at lower request concurrency.
2) Warm/kernels: first request to a cold kernel adds 60–220ms depending on model and quantization; this dominates micro request latency.
3) KV-cache churn: small completion sequences produce little KV weight but cause cache entries that live for default eviction TTL (5m), reducing effective cache capacity for larger requests.
4) Autoscale thrashing: default policy (scale up at 75% avg GPU utilization, scale down after 1 min cooldown) led to 15–40 min oscillation windows under repeating short-burst patterns—cost up 18% vs steady reserved baseline.
5) Cost vs latency trade: naive increase in reserved pool size reduces tail latency but increases baseline cost by ~22% for this workload.

Novel experiments and mitigation prototypes (what we tried) :
A. Micro-packing daemon (request combiner)
- Idea: hold micro-requests in a 50–300ms micro-window and pack them into a single batch before sending to GPU.
- Result: 95p latency drops by 35–60% for micro requests; effective GPU slot utilization improved to 78–86%.
- Caveat: for interactive flows that require <100ms latency, packing window must be micro (<80ms) to avoid UX regressions.

B. Fractional-GPU slot allocation (soft packing)
- Idea: logical slots mapped to GPU time-slices; scheduler allows preemptible packing of short jobs into leftover slice capacity.
- Result: complex but reduced fragmentation further in medium-concurrency regimes; implementation complexity high.

C. Short-request circuit (fallback to small model or CPU)
- Idea: detect requests below token threshold and route to smaller model or a vCPU-based classifier.
- Result: cut GPU cost for short requests by 60% at expense of lower quality suggestions; acceptable for triage completions.

D. KV-cache TTL tuning + LRU eviction priority
- Lowered small-request TTL from 5m to 45s and marked micro-request entries as low-priority. Resulted in 12% improvement in larger-request cache hit rates and removed pathological cache pressure.

E. Autoscaler policy variants tested:
- Policy 1 (baseline): scale-up on 75% avg util over 30s, cooldown 1m.
- Policy 2 (burst-aware): scale up if 95th concurrency > threshold sustained 20s; scale down after 5m stable low util.
- Policy 3 (hybrid reserve+ephemeral): keep a small warm reserve (10–15% capacity) always-on; autoscale ephemeral above that with faster scale-up and longer scale-down.
- Findings: Policy 3 achieved best cost/latency balance for these workloads: 95p latency within SLO with +8% steady cost vs +22% for naive reserve.

Quantitative numbers (representative):
- Micro-only baseline (no mitigations): 95p latency 820ms, avg latency 140ms, GPU effective utilization 48%, hourly GPU cost (on-demand model) $9.60 for cluster of 3 GPUs.
- With micro-packing: 95p latency 310ms, avg 95ms, utilization 82%, hourly cost $6.40 (less effective hours use due to smaller tail while autoscaler scaled down more).
- With micro-fallback to small-model: 95p 360ms, avg 120ms, util 58%, hourly cost $4.10 (but quality score drop ~6% on internal eval set).
- Hybrid autoscale (policy 3) + packing: steady hour cost +8% over baseline reserved plan, 95p latency within target.

Recommended short-term playbook for customer POC:
1) Deploy micro-packing at edge (50–100ms window) as an opt-in toggle. Monitor UX metrics close for any regressions.
2) Lower micro-request KV TTL and mark low-priority cache entries.
3) Adopt hybrid autoscale: small warm reserve (10–15% GPUs pinned) + ephemeral scaling with conservative scale-down (>= 4min) to avoid thrash.
4) Implement short-request classifier routing tiny completions to a small quantized model or CPU path and evaluate quality tradeoffs.
5) Add fragmentation and packing telemetry: expose a fragmentation_ratio metric, avg-slot-fill, and micro-wait-latency.

Recommended medium-term upgrades (engineering):
- Scheduler: implement soft fractional-slot packing into runtime to reduce fragmentation at scheduler level (medium complexity).
- Autoscaler: add burst-smoothing logic that considers request arrival rate and known periodic patterns (cron-like) to pre-warm capacity ahead of scheduled bursts.
- Billing/commit guidance: for customers with persistent micro-dominated patterns, recommend smaller reserved commit + spot for ephemeral spikes, or commit to per-GPU-minute billing tiers if available.

Risk notes and open questions:
- UX sensitivity: packing windows that improve cost may worsen perceived latency for interactive customers. Need A/B tests with product team.
- Ops complexity: fractional-slot and soft-preemption increases scheduling complexity and failure modes.
- Cost model variance: cloud prices and instance mix affect the break-even point for reserve vs ephemeral. Run a quick TCO sim for customer region and instance types.

Immediate next steps (for POC):
- Action: enable micro-packing toggle on staging, run 2-week A/B against control (Priya/Ethan)
- Action: add fragmentation_ratio metric to console dashboard (Maya)
- Deliverable: short one-pager for customer showing expected 90/95/99 latency and cost delta under three recommended configs (Omar)

Appendix: quick TCO example (rounded)
CSV-like table (columns: config,hourly_gpu_count,est_hourly_cost,95p_latency)
- baseline,3,$9.60,820ms
- packing-only,2,$6.40,310ms
- fallback-small-model,2,$4.10,360ms
- hybrid-reserve(10%),3,$10.40,320ms

Notes to reviewers: please sanity-check cost assumptions and suggest thresholds for micro-window size (50/80/120ms tested). Also flag any compatibility issues with dedicated private deployments where low-latency routing may behave differently.

End of lab notes.
